usage: 좋아하다 takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가
the verb 좋아하다 turns into the modifier 좋아하는 placed before the noun
with 많다 the noun takes the subject marker 이, never 을
두 Sino-Korean nouns stack bare with no particle between them
examples: 저는 과목을 골라요.
I choose a subject.
simple 를 + verb: 과목 is the thing you pick
제일 좋아하는 과목은 음악이에요.
My favorite subject is music.
좋아하는 modifies 과목; 은 marks it as the topic of the sentence
이번 학기에는 과목이 너무 많아서 힘들어요.
This term there are so many subjects that it is hard.
real complaint: 많아서 (so many, therefore) links the cause to 힘들다
nuance: 과목 is a school subject as a field of study — math, science, music — the label on a curriculum, written 科目 (科 'branch/category' + 目 'item'), literally a 'category item'. Do not confuse it with 수업, which is the actual class period or lesson you sit through: you 'like a 과목' (the topic) but you 'have a 수업 at 3 o'clock' (the session). It also differs from 전공, the single 'major' you commit to at university — 과목 is any one of many courses. With descriptive adjectives like 많다 or 어렵다 it must take 이/가 (과목이 어려워요), but with 좋아하다/배우다 it takes 을/를; the English-speaker trap is forcing 'I like science' into 과목을 좋아하다 + a separate noun, when Koreans just name the subject directly (음악을 좋아해요).

mistakes: Saying 과목을 많아요 by copying English 'I have many subjects' — 많다 is descriptive, so the subject takes 이: 과목이 많아요.
Using 과목 for the class hour, e.g. 과목이 세 시예요; the timetable slot is 수업, so say 수업이 세 시에 있어요.
Translating 'my major is...' as 제 과목은...; a university major is 전공, so it should be 제 전공은....

usage: 어렵다 is descriptive, so 수학 takes the subject marker 이
배우다 (to learn) takes the object marker 을
수학 + 시간 stack bare to mean the math lesson slot
잘하다 (do well) takes 을; this is the set phrase for a skill
examples: 수학 숙제가 많아요.
There is a lot of math homework.
simple: 수학 modifies 숙제, and 많다 takes 이/가
우리는 학교에서 수학을 배워요.
We learn math at school.
를 marks what we learn; 에서 marks the place
저는 수학을 잘 못해서 학원에 다녀요.
I'm not good at math so I go to an academy.
real life: 잘 못하다 = 'not good at', 못해서 gives the reason
nuance: 수학 is the school subject mathematics, written 數學 (數 'number' + 學 'study') — literally the 'study of numbers'. The 學 ending is the standard Sino-Korean tag for an academic discipline, the same 학 in 과학, 역사학, 의학, so once you know it you can read whole subject names. Note the contrast between 수학 (the abstract discipline) and 산수, the simple 'arithmetic' little children do — adults studying equations always say 수학. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is the particle on the adjective: 'math is hard for me' feels like math is the object, but 어렵다/쉽다 are descriptive verbs, so math is the grammatical subject and takes 이 — 수학이 어려워요, never 수학을 어려워요. To express skill, use the fixed 수학을 잘하다/못하다 with 을, where the verb (not the adjective) governs the object marker.

Using 산수 (arithmetic) for the secondary-school subject; once it involves algebra say 수학.
Dropping 잘 and saying 수학을 해요 for 'I'm good at math'; you need 수학을 잘해요 to convey skill.

usage: 재미있다 is descriptive, so 과학 takes 이
공부하다 takes the object marker 을
과학 modifies 선생님 with no particle between
과학 + 실험 stack to name the lab activity
examples: 과학이 재미있어요.
Science is fun.
simple descriptive sentence: 이 marks 과학, 재미있다 follows
오늘 과학 시간에 실험을 했어요.
We did an experiment in science class today.
과학 시간 = the lesson; 실험을 하다 is the set phrase
저는 커서 과학을 더 공부하고 싶어요.
When I grow up I want to study science more.
real goal: 커서 'having grown up', 고 싶다 expresses the wish
nuance: 과학 is the school subject and the broad field of science, written 科學 (科 'branch/discipline' + 學 'study') — the 'study of disciplines', i.e. systematic knowledge. The same 과 appears in 과목 (subject) and 학과 (academic department), so the words cluster naturally. Keep 과학 (the field) separate from 과목 (any subject in general) — science is one 과목 among many; and from 기술, the 'technology/practical-skills' subject sometimes paired with it. As a noun modifier, 과학 sits bare before another noun (과학 선생님, 과학 책, 과학 실험) with no possessive particle. The English-speaker pitfall is again the adjective particle: 'science is interesting' must be 과학이 재미있어요 (subject marker), and learners also over-add 의 (과학의 선생님) where natural Korean just stacks the two nouns: 과학 선생님.

usage: 배우다 takes the object marker 를
길다 is descriptive, so 역사 takes 가
country name 한국 modifies 역사 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 를
examples: 역사를 좋아해요.
I like history.
simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 를
한국 역사는 아주 길어요.
Korean history is very long.
한국 역사 is the topic (는); 길다 describes it
역사 시험 때문에 어젯밤에 늦게까지 공부했어요.
Because of the history exam I studied late last night.
real life: 때문에 = 'because of', 늦게까지 = 'until late'
nuance: 역사 means history — both the school subject and the actual record of the past — written 歷史 (歷 'to pass through / experience' + 史 'chronicle, records'), literally 'the record of what has passed'. Distinguish it sharply from 옛날, which is the storytelling adverbial 'long ago / once upon a time': you study 역사 in class, but a folktale starts 옛날 옛적에. It also differs from 역사학, the academic 'study OF history' a scholar specializes in; the everyday school subject is plain 역사. A country's history stacks the country name bare in front — 한국 역사, 세계 역사 — with no 의 needed. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 옛날 or 과거 ('the past') when naming the class; the subject and the discipline are both 역사.

Adding 의 in 한국의 역사 by reflex; natural everyday Korean stacks them bare as 한국 역사.

usage: 배우다 takes the object marker 을
미술 + 시간 names the art lesson slot
미술 modifies 선생님 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 을
examples: 미술을 좋아해요.
I like art (class).
simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을
미술 시간에 그림을 그려요.
We draw pictures in art class.
그림을 그리다 is the fixed verb-noun pair for drawing
미술 시간에 만든 작품을 교실에 걸었어요.
We hung the work we made in art class on the wall.
real life: 만든 modifies 작품, 걸다 = 'to hang'
nuance: 미술 is the school subject of visual art — drawing, painting, making things — written 美術 (美 'beauty' + 術 'art/technique, skill'), literally the 'technique of beauty'. That same 술 'technique' appears in 기술 (technology) and 예술 (the arts), which helps you read related words. Crucially, 미술 is the subject/field, while 그림 is a concrete 'picture/drawing' you produce, and 예술 is 'the arts' in the grand sense (music, dance, literature too); a child does 미술 in school but creates a 그림. Note the set collocation 그림을 그리다 ('draw a picture'), where the noun and verb share the root 그리- and must appear together. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 미술을 그리다 ('draw art') — you draw a 그림, and you 'learn/like' 미술 (미술을 배우다/좋아하다).

usage: 좋아하다 takes the object marker 을
체육 + 시간 names the gym-class slot
있다 (to exist) takes the subject marker 이
체육 + 복 (clothes) compound for gym clothes
examples: 체육을 좋아해요.
I like PE.
simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 을
체육 시간에 축구를 했어요.
We played soccer in PE.
체육 시간 = the lesson; 축구를 하다 = play soccer
내일 체육 시간에는 체육복을 꼭 가져와야 해요.
Tomorrow for PE you must bring your gym clothes.
real life: 가져오다 = 'bring', 아/어야 하다 = 'must'
nuance: 체육 is physical education, the school subject of exercise and sport, written 體育 (體 'body' + 育 'to raise, nurture'), literally 'raising/educating the body' — a neat mirror of 교육 (敎育, 'teaching-education'). Keep 체육 (the curriculum subject) distinct from 운동, the everyday word for 'exercise / a workout / sports' in general: you have a 체육 class at school but you go 운동(을) 하다 at the gym on weekends. The compound 체육복 ('PE + clothes') is the required gym uniform, and the venue is the 체육관 (gymnasium). With 있다 the noun takes 이/가 (체육 시간이 있어요), but with 좋아하다 it takes 을/를. The English-speaker pitfall is using 운동 for the timetabled subject (운동 시간); the school slot is 체육 시간.

Saying 체육을 있어요 for 'there's PE'; 있다 needs the subject marker: 체육 시간이 있어요.

usage: 배우다 takes the object marker 를
지리 + 시간 names the geography lesson slot
country name 한국 modifies 지리 bare
공부하다 takes the object marker 를
examples: 지리를 배워요.
I learn geography.
simple: 배우다 needs the object marker 를
지리 시간에 세계 지도를 봤어요.
In geography we looked at a world map.
note the near-twins: 지리 (the subject) vs 지도 (the map)
저는 한국 지리는 잘 아는데 세계 지리는 어려워요.
I know Korean geography well but world geography is hard.
real life: 는데 contrasts the two halves
nuance: 지리 is geography, the subject about the earth's land, places, and features, written 地理 (地 'earth/ground' + 理 'principle, pattern'), literally 'the patterns of the land'. The 地 'earth' element ties it to 지도 (地圖, 'earth-map'), 지구 (地球, 'earth-globe'), and 지진 (地震, 'earth-quake'), so the cluster is learnable as a family. The trap pair is 지리 vs 지도: 지리 is the field of study (the knowledge), while 지도 is a physical map you hold or look at — in 지리 class you study a 지도. As a modifier, region names stack bare: 한국 지리, 세계 지리. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 지도 for the subject (지도를 배워요, 'learn the map'), or adding 의 (한국의 지리) where bare stacking is more natural.

usage: 좋다 is descriptive, so 성적 takes 이
나오다 (come out) takes the subject marker 이
받다 (receive) takes the object marker 을
오르다 (rise) takes the subject marker 이
examples: 성적이 좋아요.
My grades are good.
simple descriptive: 좋다 takes the subject marker 이
다음 주에 성적이 나와요.
The grades come out next week.
성적이 나오다 = results are released/posted
이번에 성적이 많이 올라서 부모님이 정말 기뻐하셨어요.
My grades went up a lot this time so my parents were really pleased.
real life: 올라서 gives the reason; 기뻐하시다 (honorific) for parents
nuance: 성적 means academic grades, marks, or results, written 成績 (成 'to accomplish, achieve' + 績 'achievement, merit'), literally 'accomplished achievements' — the outcome of your effort. Distinguish it from 점수, a single numeric 'score' on one test (시험 점수 90점), and from 시험, the 'exam' itself: you take a 시험, get a 점수 on it, and your overall 성적 reflects the term. Note the directional verbs that pair with it: 성적이 나오다 (results 'come out'/are released), 성적을 받다 (you 'receive' them), 성적이 오르다/떨어지다 (they rise/fall). The English-speaker pitfall is using 시험 where you mean the resulting grade ('my exam was good' → say 성적이 좋아요), and choosing the wrong particle: with descriptive 좋다 or motion 나오다/오르다 it's 이/가, only with 받다 is it 을/를.

usage: 몇 ('how many') + 학년 asks the year level
Sino-Korean number 일 + 학년 (note: 일 not 한)
올라가다 (go up) takes the subject marker 이
examples: 저는 일 학년이에요.
I'm in first grade.
Sino number 일 + 학년; 이에요 states the fact
동생은 지금 몇 학년이에요?
What grade is your sibling in now?
몇 학년 = 'which grade', the standard question
내년에 삼 학년이 되면 공부가 더 어려워질 거예요.
When I become a third-grader next year, studying will get harder.
real life: 이 되면 = 'when (one) becomes', 어려워지다 = 'get harder'
nuance: 학년 means a school grade or year level (1st year, 2nd year), written 學年 (學 'study' + 年 'year'), literally 'study-year'. Two things trip up English speakers. First, 학년 always counts with SINO-Korean numbers — 일 학년, 이 학년, 삼 학년 — never the native set (not 한 학년 for 'first grade'; 한 학년 means 'one grade-level' as in 한 학년 위, 'one year above'). Second, keep 학년 (the grade/year you're in) separate from 학교 (the school building/institution) and from 학기 (學期, the 'semester/term' within a year): you're in 이 학년 at your 학교 during the spring 학기. To ask, use 몇 학년 ('which grade'). With 되다/올라가다 the noun takes 이/가 (삼 학년이 되다, 학년이 올라가다), and as a count noun before 이에요 you simply state 일 학년이에요.

mistakes: Saying 한 학년이에요 for 'I'm in first grade'; grade levels use Sino numbers: 일 학년이에요.
Confusing 학년 with 학기; the year level is 학년, but a semester is 학기 (e.g. 이번 학기).
Asking 무슨 학년이에요?; the natural question word for a number is 몇, so say 몇 학년이에요?

usage: 전공 + 뭐 (what) asks the field of study
정하다 (decide) takes the object marker 을
바꾸다 (change) takes the object marker 을
전공 modifies 수업 to mean a course in one's major
examples: 제 전공은 한국어예요.
My major is Korean.
전공 + 은 marks the topic; 이에요/예요 states it
전공이 뭐예요?
What's your major?
the everyday question to a university student
저는 전공을 경제학에서 심리학으로 바꿨어요.
I changed my major from economics to psychology.
real life: 에서...으로 = 'from...to', 바꾸다 = change
nuance: 전공 is your academic major — the single specialized field you concentrate on at university — written 專攻 (專 'exclusive, sole' + 攻 'to attack, devote effort to'), literally 'to devote oneself exclusively', i.e. to specialize. It can also act as a verb with 하다: 한국어를 전공하다 ('to major in Korean'). The key contrast is 전공 vs 과목: a 과목 is any one of the many courses on your timetable, whereas 전공 is the one field you commit to — you take many 과목 but have one 전공. It also differs from 학과, the 'academic department' that houses the major. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a major 과목 (제 과목은..., wrong) and forgetting that with the verb form the field takes 을/를: not 한국어 전공해요 but 한국어를 전공해요; as a plain noun, though, 전공이 뭐예요 uses 이/가.

usage: 다니다 (commute/attend) takes the destination marker 에
끝나다 (end) takes the subject marker 이
subject name 영어 modifies 학원 bare
끝나다 + 고 = 'after it ends', then do the next thing
examples: 저는 영어 학원에 다녀요.
I go to an English academy.
학원에 다니다 = attend regularly; 에 marks where you go
학원이 아홉 시에 끝나요.
The academy lets out at nine.
끝나다 takes 이/가; 에 marks the clock time
학교 끝나고 바로 학원에 가야 해서 너무 피곤해요.
I have to go straight to the academy after school so I'm exhausted.
real life: a very Korean routine; 가야 해서 gives the reason
nuance: 학원 is a private after-school academy (cram school) where students pay for extra lessons — English, math, piano, taekwondo — written 學院 (學 'study' + 院 'institution, hall'). The 院 'institution' element links it to 병원 (病院 hospital), 대학원 (大學院 graduate school), and 미용원/미장원, so the family is learnable. Sharply distinguish 학원 (a supplementary private institute) from 학교 (學校, the regular public/formal school) and from 대학원 (graduate school) — a child attends 학교 by day and 학원 in the evening. The verb of choice is 다니다, which implies habitual commuting/membership, with the 에 particle: 학원에 다니다 ('attend an academy regularly'), not the one-off 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 학교 for any place of learning, or marking the destination with 를 (학원를 다녀요, wrong) instead of 에.

usage: 유학(을) 가다 is the set phrase; 가다 = go there
고 싶다 attaches to 가다 to express the wish
유학 + 생활 names the study-abroad lifestyle
유학(을) 오다 = come (here) to study, from the host's view
examples: 저는 일본으로 유학을 가요.
I'm going to Japan to study abroad.
으로 marks the direction; 유학(을) 가다 is the fixed phrase
언니는 미국으로 유학을 갔어요.
My older sister went to America to study abroad.
past 갔어요; the destination takes 으로/로
몇 년 동안 유학을 다녀와서 한국어가 정말 유창해요.
Having spent a few years studying abroad, her Korean is really fluent.
real life: 다녀오다 = 'go and come back', 유창하다 = fluent
nuance: 유학 means going abroad to study, usually for a degree or a long course, written 留學 (留 'to stay, remain' + 學 'study'), literally 'to remain (somewhere) and study' — note the 留 'stay', which signals it's a sustained stay, not a quick visit. That 留 distinguishes it from 여행 (旅行 'travel'), a trip for leisure: you go on 여행 for a week but go on 유학 for years. It pairs with directional verbs and the destination particle 으로/로: 유학을 가다 (go away to study), 유학을 오다 (come to study, from the host country's angle), 유학을 다녀오다 (go and return). It can also be a verb: 미국에서 유학하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 여행 for academic study abroad, and marking the country with 에 instead of 으로/로 (일본에 유학을 가요 sounds off; say 일본으로 유학을 가요).
